Section 2.7 of Lock⁵ is about what a picture gains when it carries **more than two
variables**. A scatterplot can be **augmented** with color or marker *shape* for a
categorical third variable, or with *bubble size* for a quantitative third variable;
the data can be split into **panels** (small multiples) or given separate regression
lines within groups; spaghetti plots, time-series windows, maps, heat maps, dot maps,
mountain charts, scatterplot matrices, and 3-D scatterplots handle time, geography,
and many variables at once. Adding a third variable can even **reverse** what the
two-variable picture seemed to say — **Simpson's Paradox**, which this section
illustrates with an augmented scatterplot (Exercise 2.270) and a famous kidney-stone
study (Exercise 2.300). The exercises also train a critical eye: a different time
window (Exercise 2.274) or a comparison of group means instead of within-group trends
(Exercise 2.310) can make the same data tell a different story.
Exercises 2.270–2.318 mix figure reading, exploration of online visualizations, and
hands-on work with Lock5 datasets. Tabs based on Lock5 data files include a small
executable EDA.

```{python}
#| include: false

from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():

os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
```

## Exercise 2.270

**Considering Direction of Association.** *(Figures 2.92–2.93 show a scatterplot of
Variable1 vs Variable2, alone, with a regression line, and then split by a third
variable Variable3 with groups A–D.)*

- **(a)** Two variables, both **quantitative**: Variable1 spans about 13–29 and
  Variable2 about 65–160.
- **(b)** In Figure 2.92(a) the association appears **positive** — Variable2 tends to
  rise as Variable1 rises.
- **(c)** The **response variable is Variable2** (plotted on the vertical axis, so the
  regression line predicts it from Variable1). The line shows a **positive**
  association.
- **(d)** Variable3 is **categorical**, with **four categories** (groups A, B, C, D).
- **(e)** Within *each* group — A, B, C, and D — the association between Variable1 and
  Variable2 appears **negative**.
- **(f)** All four regression lines in Figure 2.93(b) slope **downward** (negative)
  within their groups.
- **(g)** The direction of association **reverses**: ignoring Variable3 the trend is
  positive (Figure 2.92), yet within every one of the four groups the trend is
  negative. The groups occupy different parts of the plot (A low on both axes, D high
  on both), and that between-group structure creates the overall positive trend. This
  is Simpson's Paradox for quantitative variables.

## Exercise 2.271

**Visualizing the Happy Planet Index.** *(Figure 2.94 plots Happiness vs Footprint,
colored by Region: 1 = Latin America, 2 = Western nations, 3 = Middle East,
4 = Sub-Saharan Africa, 5 = South Asia, 6 = East Asia, 7 = former Communist
countries.)*

- **(a)** Happiness and Footprint are **quantitative**; Region is **categorical**
  (7 categories).
- **(b)** The two regions with the greatest happiness are **region 1 (Latin America)**
  and **region 2 (Western nations)** — their dots sit highest on the vertical axis.
  The greatest ecological footprint belongs to **region 2 (Western nations)**, far to
  the right of everyone else. (Group means: Happiness 6.9 for region 1 and 7.6 for
  region 2; Footprint 6.0 for region 2 vs ≤ 3.0 for all others.)
- **(c)** The lowest happiness belongs to **region 4 (Sub-Saharan Africa)**, and the
  ecological footprint there tends to be very **low** (mean about 1.4).
- **(d)** Ignoring region, the relationship between happiness and footprint is
  **positive** (correlation about 0.64).
- **(e)** Within region 2 alone the relationship is still **positive** (correlation
  about 0.51).
- **(f)** Costa Rica, the happiest country, sits in the **top left**: maximum
  happiness (8.5) with a small footprint (2.3).
- **(g)** For region 4 the binding constraint is well-being: focus on **Happiness and
  try to increase it** (the footprint is already tiny). For region 2 happiness is
  already high, so focus on the **Footprint and try to decrease it** — moving those
  countries toward the top left means shrinking their ecological impact, not raising
  their happiness.

*Data:* `data/ch02/HappyPlanetIndex.csv` (n = 143), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/HappyPlanetIndex.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Happiness score versus ecological footprint, colored by world region
hp = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/HappyPlanetIndex.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=hp, x="Footprint", y="Happiness", hue="Region",
                palette="tab10", s=18, alpha=0.85, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Ecological footprint")
ax.set_ylabel("Happiness score")
ax.legend(title="Region", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.272

**Height, Weight, and Body Fat.** *(Figure 2.95 shows a bubble plot of height, weight,
and body fat percentage for 100 men, from the dataset BodyFat; bubble size indicates
body fat percentage.)*

- **(a)** Three variables, all **quantitative**: height, weight, and body fat
  percentage.
- **(b)** Ignoring bubble size, height and weight show a **positive** relationship
  (correlation about 0.57).
- **(c)** The bubbles tend to be **larger on the top half** of the plot: heavier men
  tend to have higher body fat percentages (correlation between weight and body fat
  about 0.6).
- **(d)** The man weighing about 140 lb has the **larger** body fat percentage. In the
  data the ≈ 66-inch, 127-lb man has 4.0% body fat, while the ≈ 66-inch, 143-lb man
  has 11.8%.
- **(e)** Between the two ≈ 125-lb men, the **shorter** one (66 in) has the larger body
  fat percentage: 17.0% at 65.75 inches vs 4.0% at 66.75 inches.
- **(f)** The heaviest man (263 lb) has 34.5% body fat — **relatively large** (one of
  the biggest bubbles on the plot).
- **(g)** The tallest man (77.75 in) has a body fat percentage that is **pretty
  average** (17.4%), and the third-tallest (76 in) has one that is **relatively
  small** (7.8%). Being tall does not by itself go with high body fat in this sample.
- **(h)** Incorporate sex by using **color (or shape) of the bubbles** for males and
  females — or by drawing separate side-by-side panels, one for each sex.

*Data:* `data/ch02/BodyFat.csv` (n = 100), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/BodyFat.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Height and weight of 100 men, with bubble size showing body fat percentage
bf = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/BodyFat.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
ax.scatter(bf.Height, bf.Weight, s=bf.Bodyfat * 28, alpha=0.5,
           color="#4c72b0", edgecolor="white")
ax.set_xlabel("Height (inches)")
ax.set_ylabel("Weight (pounds)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.273

**Visualizing Football and Brain Size.** *(Years playing football and hippocampus size
were recorded for football players with at least one concussion, football players with
no concussion diagnosis, and a control group that never played football; Figure 2.96
plots all three variables.)*

- **(a)** Years playing football — **quantitative**; hippocampus size —
  **quantitative**; group (Control / FBConcuss / FBNoConcuss) — **categorical**.
- **(b)** The blue control dots are stacked on the left because **none of them ever
  played football**: every control case has Years = 0.
- **(c)** Overall there appears to be a **negative** association: people who played
  football for more years tend to have smaller hippocampi.
- **(d)** The **concussion group (FBConcuss)** has the lower regression line: at the
  same number of years of football, players with a concussion diagnosis have smaller
  hippocampi than players without one (group means: about 5735 vs 6459).
- **(e)** The **non-concussion group** has the steeper slope: about −115 mm³ of
  hippocampus per year played, versus about −55 mm³ per year for the concussion group
  (computed from the data).

*Data:* `data/ch02/FootballBrain.csv` (n = 75), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/FootballBrain.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Hippocampus size versus years playing football, by group, with regression lines for the two football groups
fb = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/FootballBrain.csv")
palette = {"Control": "#55a868", "FBNoConcuss": "#4c72b0", "FBConcuss": "#c44e52"}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=fb, x="Years", y="Hipp", hue="Group", palette=palette,
                s=22, alpha=0.75, ax=ax)
for g in ["FBNoConcuss", "FBConcuss"]:
    sns.regplot(data=fb[fb.Group == g], x="Years", y="Hipp", scatter=False,
                ax=ax, color=palette[g], truncate=True, line_kws={"lw": 2})
ax.set_xlabel("Years playing football")
ax.set_ylabel("Hippocampus size")
ax.legend(title="Group", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.274

**Carbon Dioxide Levels Over Time.** *(Figure 2.97 shows atmospheric CO2 over
1959–2015 and, in a very different window, over the last 400,000 years.)*

- **(a)** From Figure 2.97(a), the CO2 concentration in 1960 is about **315–317 ppm**
  and in 2015 about **400 ppm**.
- **(b)** During 1959–2015 the concentration is **increasing** — steadily and without
  interruption.
- **(c)** Over the 400,000-year window the concentration is **oscillating up and
  down**: repeated ice-age cycles between roughly 180 and 280 ppm.
- **(d)** The 1959–2015 stretch is a **nearly vertical spike at the far right edge**
  of Figure 2.97(b) — a thin sliver of time in which CO2 shoots up past every level
  seen in the previous 400,000 years.
- **(e)** The highest concentration before 1950 is about **280–300 ppm**, reached at
  the warm interglacial peaks.
- **(f)** The 3-minute animated video referenced in the exercise animates this same
  story: centuries of oscillation followed by the recent sharp climb.

*Data:* `data/ch02/CarbonDioxide.csv` (CO2 in ppm, every 5 years, 1960–2015),
downloaded from <https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/CarbonDioxide.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Atmospheric CO2 concentration, 1960 to 2015
cd = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/CarbonDioxide.csv")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
ax.plot(cd.Year, cd["C02"], marker="o", ms=3, color="#4c72b0")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("CO2 (ppm)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.275

**Forty-Yard Dash at the NFL Combine.** *(Figure 2.98 is a spaghetti plot of the
average 40-yard dash time by season, 1990–2016, for wide receivers (WR) and defensive
cornerbacks (DC).)*

- **(a)** Both strands wander a lot from year to year, but their general trend is
  **downward** — from about 4.52–4.56 seconds in the 1990s to about 4.45–4.50 seconds
  in the 2010s. The players are getting **faster**, not slower.
- **(b)** In 2016 the **DC** strand ends slightly lower (about 4.46 s vs about 4.48 s
  for WR), so defensive cornerbacks had the faster average 40 time that year.
- **(c)** No — the two strands **cross repeatedly** over the 27 seasons. Neither
  position is consistently faster than the other; the common assumption that receivers
  are always the speedsters does not hold up in these averages.

## Exercise 2.278

**Marriage Age vs Number of Children.** *(Gapminder scatterplot of Age at 1st marriage
(women) vs Babies per woman, animated over time.)*

- **(a)** Overall there is a **negative** association: countries where women marry
  later tend to have fewer babies per woman.
- **(b)** In Russia, 1941–1943 (World War II), **both variables plunge**: the mean
  number of babies per woman drops steeply, and the age at 1st marriage also falls
  sharply as wartime upheaval rushes marriages forward while births collapse.
- **(c)** In Libya, 1973–2005, the classic development pattern plays out: the number
  of babies per woman **falls dramatically** (from about 7–8 toward 3), while the age
  at 1st marriage **rises substantially** as women marry later and later.

## Exercise 2.279

**Income Distribution by Country.** *(Gapminder mountain chart: a smoothed histogram
of world income for each year, with the area under the curve colored by region.)*

- **(a)** In 1970, the majority of people living in extreme poverty (under \$2/day)
  came from **Asia** — the huge low-income humps of China and the rest of South and
  East Asia dominate the bottom of the distribution.
- **(b)** By 2019, the majority of people in extreme poverty came from **Africa**,
  whose colored area now sits lowest on the income axis.
- **(c)** In 1970 the worldwide income distribution is strongly **bimodal**: a very
  large, low-income peak (the developing world) plus a much smaller, separate peak of
  wealthy countries. By 2019 the two humps have merged into one broad distribution
  centered on **middle incomes** — the poor peak has shrunk and moved right, and a
  global middle class has swelled.

## Exercise 2.290

**A Scatterplot Matrix.** *(Figure 2.102 shows scatterplots for every pair of
quantitative variables, colored by Type.)*

- **(a)** The **petal length vs petal width** scatterplot separates Versicolor and
  Virginica much more clearly: their points interlock almost completely in the sepal
  length vs sepal width panel, but form distinct (if partly overlapping) bands in the

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Scatterplot matrix of the four iris measurements, colored by type

             vars=["PetalWidth", "PetalLength", "SepalWidth", "SepalLength"],
             height=1.35, aspect=1.05, plot_kws={"s": 12})

```

## Exercise 2.291

**A 3-Dimensional Scatterplot.** *(Figure 2.103 plots petal length, petal width, and
sepal length together.)*

- **Sepal length is on the vertical axis.** The dots highest up are the **Virginica**
  irises (mean sepal length about 66 mm, versus 59 mm for Versicolor and 50 mm for
  Setosa); the Setosa dots sit lowest.

*Data:* `data/ch02/FisherIris.csv` (n = 150):

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Petal length, petal width, and sepal length in a 3-dimensional scatterplot
from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D  # noqa: F401
colors3d = {"Setosa": "#4c72b0", "Versicolor": "#dd8452", "Virginica": "#55a868"}
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, 4))
ax = fig.add_subplot(111, projection="3d")
for t, d in fi.groupby("Type"):
    ax.scatter(d.PetalWidth, d.PetalLength, d.SepalLength, s=12, alpha=0.7,
               color=colors3d[t], label=t)
ax.set_xlabel("Petal width (mm)")
ax.set_ylabel("Petal length (mm)")
ax.set_zlabel("Sepal length (mm)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**U.S. Age Pyramid Becomes a Rectangle.** *(Pew's animated age-sex histograms of the

- **(a)** In 1950 the age distribution has a **very wide base**: many children, with
  counts shrinking at every older age (the baby-boom cohort forms a bulge at the
  bottom).

  women live longer.

## Exercise 2.295

**Are Carbon or Steel Bikes Faster?** *(Dr. Groves flipped a coin each day for 56
commutes between a 20.9 lb carbon bike and a 29.75 lb steel bike; data in BikeCommute.)*

- **(a)** The most obvious difference in Figure 2.104 is that the **distances were not
  the same** for the two bikes: carbon-bike commutes cluster around 27.3–27.5 miles,
  while steel-bike commutes spread lower (about 25.9–27.4; means 27.37 vs 26.98 miles).
- **(b)** Average speed is time divided by distance. The carbon bike's higher average
  speed (15.19 vs 15.04 mph) is exactly what its longer distances produce in total
  time: more miles at a slightly faster pace still means more minutes (108.3 vs
  107.8 min on average). The two summaries disagree only because the distances differ.
- **(c)** The confounding variable is the **commute distance** (which routes, hence
  which distances, happened to be ridden on each bike) — it is associated with which
  bike was used and directly determines the commute time.
- **(d)** Compare the bikes over the **same distance** — and since the carbon bike is
  genuinely faster per mile, ride the carbon bike (on the shortest sensible route) to
  minimize commute time.

*Data:* `data/ch02/BikeCommute.csv` (n = 56), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/BikeCommute.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Commute time versus distance, by type of bike
bc = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/BikeCommute.csv")
bc = bc.loc[:, ~bc.columns.str.startswith("Unnamed")]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=bc, x="Distance", y="Minutes", hue="Bike",
                palette={"Steel": "#c44e52", "Carbon": "#4c72b0"},
                s=28, alpha=0.8, ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel("Commute distance (miles)")
ax.set_ylabel("Commute time (minutes)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.298

**Does Buying Organic Food Improve Your Health? Or Is It Income?** *(NHANES survey
data: people who bought organic were more likely to report very good or excellent
health.)*

- **(a)** People who bought organic food have **higher incomes**: in the data, the
  share buying organic climbs from about 26% in the lowest income band to about 56% in
  the highest (correlation between buying organic and income about 0.19), and the
  organic-buyers' income boxplot in Figure 2.105 sits well above the non-buyers'.
- **(b)** Health status also **rises with income**: the proportion reporting very good
  or excellent health increases steadily from about 31% in the lowest income category
  to about 62% in the highest, with point size showing how many people each category
  contains.
- **(c)** Income is associated with the explanatory variable (buying organic — part
  a) **and** influences the response (health status — part b). That is exactly the
  definition of a **confounding variable** for the organic–health association.
- **(d) No.** This is an observational survey — nobody was assigned to buy organic —
  so even with income identified, confounding (in whole or part) cannot be ruled out
  and a causal conclusion is not warranted.

*Data:* `data/ch01/NHANES.csv` (NHANES 2009–2010 subset, n = 4716), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/NHANES.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 3.5))
sns.boxplot(data=nh, x="Organic", y="Income", ax=ax, color="#4c72b0", width=0.45)
ax.set_xlabel("Bought organic food")
ax.set_ylabel("Monthly income (USD)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Proportion reporting very good or excellent health by monthly income
nh2 = nh.assign(Band=(nh.Income // 1000) * 1000 + 500)
g = nh2[nh2.Band < 10500].groupby("Band").agg(
    n=("HealthBinary", "size"),
    p=("HealthBinary", lambda s: (s == "Very good / Excellent").mean()))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
ax.plot(g.index, g.p, color="#4c72b0", lw=1, alpha=0.7)
ax.scatter(g.index, g.p, s=g.n / 3, color="#4c72b0", alpha=0.65)
ax.set_ylim(0.2, 0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Monthly income (USD, band midpoint)")
ax.set_ylabel("Proportion with very good or excellent health")
```

## Exercise 2.299

**Organic and Health: Breaking it Down by Income.** *(Figure 2.107 compares organic
buyers and non-buyers on health within each income group.)*

- **(a)** Yes, generally. Within most income groups the organic buyers still report
  better health — e.g., in the lowest income band about 43% of organic buyers report
  very good or excellent health vs about 27% of non-buyers, and in the highest band
  about 69% vs 53%. The within-group differences are smaller and noisier than the
  overall gap (one middle band even flips), but the organic advantage does not vanish.
- **(b) No — not conclusively.** Breaking the data down by income removes much of
  income's confounding effect, but income is only *one* of many possible confounders
  (health consciousness, education, access to care, ...). The study is still
  observational, the health measure is self-reported, and the small within-group
  samples are noisy — so a causal conclusion is still not justified.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Proportion with very good or excellent health by income group, broken down by organic purchase
g2 = nh2[nh2.Band < 10500].groupby(["Organic", "Band"], observed=True).agg(
    n=("HealthBinary", "size"),
    p=("HealthBinary", lambda s: (s == "Very good / Excellent").mean()))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5))
for lbl, col in [("Yes", "#4c72b0"), ("No", "#c44e52")]:
    d = g2.xs(lbl, level="Organic")
    ax.plot(d.index, d.p, color=col, lw=1.2, alpha=0.8)
    ax.scatter(d.index, d.p, s=d.n / 2.5, color=col, alpha=0.7,
               label="Bought organic" if lbl == "Yes" else "Did not buy organic")
ax.set_ylim(0.15, 0.75)
ax.set_xlabel("Monthly income (USD, band midpoint)")
ax.set_ylabel("Proportion with very good or excellent health")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.300

**Kidney Stone Treatment.** *(A study compared open surgery and percutaneous
nephrolithotomy for kidney stones, with success = stones eliminated or under 2 mm
after three months. Figure 2.108 shows success and failure counts, overall and broken
down by stone size.)*

- **(a)** Considering all stones, **percutaneous nephrolithotomy** is more successful:
  289/350 = **83%** vs 273/350 = **78%** for open surgery.
- **(b)** For **small stones, open surgery** wins: 81/87 = **93%** vs 234/270 =
  **87%**.
- **(c)** For **large stones, open surgery** also wins: 192/263 = **73%** vs 55/80 =
  **69%**.
- **(d)** **Small stones** produce higher success rates under both treatments.
- **(e)** **Percutaneous nephrolithotomy** was more commonly used for small stones
  (270 of its 350 cases) — doctors preferred the less invasive procedure when stones
  were small.
- **(f)** **Open surgery** was more commonly used for large stones (263 of its 350
  cases).
- **(g) Simpson's Paradox.** Stone size is associated with both the treatment chosen
  and the success rate: open surgery was mostly applied to *large* stones (hard cases,
  lower success for anyone) while percutaneous nephrolithotomy was mostly applied to
  *small* stones (easy cases). Aggregating over stone size, the easy-case treatment
  piles up successes and looks better overall — even though open surgery is better
  within *each* stone-size group.
- **(h)** Almost certainly **not** a randomized experiment. Treatment was tied
  systematically to stone size (large stones got open surgery), which randomization
  would prevent; this is an observational comparison of treatments as doctors chose
  them.

*Data (counts read from Figure 2.108):*

```{python}
#| echo: false
ks = pd.DataFrame({
    "Stones": ["All", "All", "Small", "Small", "Large", "Large"],
    "Treatment": ["Open surgery", "Percutaneous", "Open surgery",
                  "Percutaneous", "Open surgery", "Percutaneous"],
    "Success": [273, 289, 81, 234, 192, 55],
    "Failure": [77, 61, 6, 36, 71, 25],
})
ks["SuccessRate"] = (ks.Success / (ks.Success + ks.Failure)).round(3)
ks
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Kidney stone success rates by treatment and stone size
ks["Stones"] = pd.Categorical(ks["Stones"], categories=["All", "Small", "Large"],
                              ordered=True)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
sns.barplot(data=ks, x="Stones", y="SuccessRate", hue="Treatment", ax=ax,
            hue_order=["Open surgery", "Percutaneous"],
            palette=["#4c72b0", "#c44e52"])
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xlabel("Stone size")
ax.set_ylabel("Success rate")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.310

**Faculty Salary, Completion Rate, and Control.** *(CollegeScores4yr: monthly faculty
salary and six-year graduation rate for four-year colleges, split Public vs Private,
omitting for-profit schools.)*

- **(a)** **Public** schools have the higher mean monthly faculty salary: about
  \$8520 vs about \$7091 for private schools.
- **(b)** **Private** schools have the higher mean completion rate: about 55.7% vs
  50.2%.
- **(c)** Based only on those means, you would expect completion rates to **decrease**
  as faculty salaries increase — the group with the higher salary (public) has the
  lower completion rate.
- **(d)** The **blue circles and solid blue regression line represent Private**
  colleges (they cluster at the lower salaries), with public colleges in the dashed
  red line.
- **(e) No — the opposite.** Within *both* types of school the association is strongly
  **positive** (correlation about 0.65 for each), directly contradicting the negative
  expectation built from the group means. Comparing means across groups and comparing
  trends within groups lead to opposite conclusions — the same aggregation reversal
  that underlies Simpson's Paradox.

*Data:* `data/ch02/CollegeScores4yr.csv` (n = 1842 four-year colleges; 1243 private
and 599 public), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/CollegeScores4yr.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
cs = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/CollegeScores4yr.csv")
cs = cs[cs.Control.isin(["Public", "Private"])]
cs.groupby("Control")[["FacSalary", "CompRate"]].mean().round(1)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Completion rate versus monthly faculty salary, private and public four-year colleges
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
sns.scatterplot(data=cs, x="FacSalary", y="CompRate", hue="Control", s=12,
                alpha=0.45, palette={"Private": "#4c72b0", "Public": "#c44e52"},
                ax=ax)
for ctl, col in [("Private", "#4c72b0"), ("Public", "#c44e52")]:
    sns.regplot(data=cs[cs.Control == ctl], x="FacSalary", y="CompRate",
                scatter=False, ax=ax, color=col, line_kws={"lw": 2, "ls": "--"})
ax.set_xlabel("Monthly faculty salary (USD)")
ax.set_ylabel("Completion rate (percent)")
ax.legend(title="Control", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 2.315

**Monthly City Temperatures.** *(CityTemps: average monthly temperature for Moscow,
Melbourne, and San Francisco — the data file covers 2017–2018.)*

- **(a)** **Moscow vs San Francisco:** Moscow swings enormously through the year —
  from about −9 °C in winter to about +20 °C in summer — while San Francisco stays
  mild and flat (roughly 10–21 °C all year). Moscow is far colder in winter and only
  a little warmer in summer; its seasonal range is about four times as wide.
- **(b)** **Melbourne vs San Francisco:** the two cities have similar annual averages
  (about 15 °C) but **opposite seasons** — Melbourne (Southern Hemisphere) is warmest
  in December–February, exactly when San Francisco is coolest, and coolest in
  June–August when San Francisco peaks. The two curves are nearly mirror images.

*Data:* `data/ch02/CityTemps.csv` (24 monthly observations, 2017–2018), downloaded
from <https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/CityTemps.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Average monthly temperature for Moscow, Melbourne, and San Francisco
ct = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/CityTemps.csv")
ct_long = ct.melt(id_vars=["Year", "Month"], var_name="City", value_name="Temp")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
sns.lineplot(data=ct_long, x="Month", y="Temp", hue="City", style="Year",
             markers=True, dashes=True, ax=ax)
ax.set_xticks(range(1, 13))
ax.set_xlabel("Month")
ax.set_ylabel("Average temperature (C)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
